cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-bnf-christ-f.summary: Over a dense grid of Latin capitals, the figure of Christ stands frontally with arms stretched wide in the form of the cross, wearing a loincloth, his cross-nimbus and body outlined so that the letters inside them form separate verses. Christ's own body becomes the text: word and image together proclaim him as Saviour on the Cross. It is the opening and best-known figure of Rabanus's cycle.
facts: Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda and later Archbishop of Mainz, composed this cycle of figure-poems (carmina figurata) in praise of the Cross around 810; each page is a grid of letters in which shapes pick out further verses.
According to the Commons description, this copy was offered to the abbey of Saint-Denis between 845 and 847.
The last poem of the cycle shows Rabanus himself kneeling before the Cross.
cur:manuscripts-de-laudibus-bnf-christ-f.notes: Shelfmark not stated on the Commons file (another Commons photograph names BnF Latin 2423 for a copy of the same work).

cur:manuscripts-gero-codex-christ-in-maj.summary: Christ, youthful and haloed, sits frontally on a cushioned throne within a great blue disc framed by a golden scale-patterned ring, blessing and holding a book on his knee; the four evangelist symbols appear in medallions at the cardinal points. The composition is closely modelled on the Majestas of the Carolingian Lorsch Gospels, reinterpreted in the early Ottonian style.
facts: The Gero Codex was probably produced at Reichenau between 950 and 970 and is one of the first and most splendid works of the 'Eburnant group' of early Ottonian manuscripts.
Its Christ in Majesty is copied from a Carolingian model, the Lorsch Gospels, and was in turn borrowed by the Petershausen Sacramentary.

cur:manuscripts-new-minster-charter-chri.summary: In the upper part of a page framed with acanthus, Christ sits in a mandorla held aloft by four angels, holding a book; below, King Edgar, between the Virgin Mary and St Peter — patrons of the New Minster — raises the charter up toward him. The image makes the king's grant an offering to Christ himself.
facts: The New Minster Charter commemorates Edgar's conversion of the New Minster, Winchester, into a Benedictine monastery in 966; every page is written in gold, which was unusual in England.
This frontispiece is the charter's only fully illuminated page and is among the earliest works of the Winchester School.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-86-nativi.summary: Under the Hand of God the Nativity takes place within a walled enclosure: the infant Christ, cross-nimbed, is bathed by two midwives with an angel's help, while crowds fill the 'gates of Sion' outside. Below, men with scrolls and a harp gaze up at the scene. The illustrator read the verse 'this man was born there' as a prophecy of Christ's birth in Zion.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-86-nativi.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-150-chris.summary: In the centre of the drawing the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos stands in a mandorla among six angels with bannered wands, carrying a bannered cross-staff over his shoulder and raising his right hand. Around him people praise him with trumpets, psaltery, harps and cymbals, and below an elaborate pipe organ with huge bellows is worked by four men while two others play it. The page is a famous source for Carolingian musical instruments.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.

The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:monumental-hagia-sophia-apse-virgin-.summary: High in the gold semi-dome of the apse, the Virgin in a dark blue maphorion sits on a jewelled, backless throne with green cushions, holding the Christ Child, who sits upright on her lap in robes of gold, raising his hand in blessing. Her calm, frontal gaze and the gentle naturalism of the faces mark one of the first great images set up in Constantinople after the end of Iconoclasm.
facts: The mosaic is usually connected with a homily delivered by Patriarch Photius in Hagia Sophia on 29 March 867, though some scholars argue for earlier or later dates.
It was rediscovered by the Fossati brothers in 1847–1848 and uncovered by Thomas Whittemore's restoration in 1935–1939.
A menologion icon at Saint Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, includes a very similar image labelled in Georgian as 'of the semi-dome of Hagia Sophia'.
